chapter_theme: Gandharvadattai is carried through the sky with a vast army whose elephants out-roar the clouds; Dharan reveals to Sridattan that his shipwreck was a ruse made at Kaluzhavegan's bidding after an astrologer's word, shows him his ship and companions safe, and Sridattan brings the princess home to Rajamapuram, tells his wife, and gains the king's consent for her marriage rite.

cast.role: a merchant of Rajamapuram, friend of the vidyadhara king
the vidyadhara who staged Sridattan's wreck and brought him to the Silver Mountain
the vidyadhara king of the Silver Mountain, Gandharvadattai's father
kings who sought Gandharvadattai on the Silver Mountain
the usurping minister, now ruling Rajamapuram as king

565.reading: The only daughter of the victorious vidyadhara king sets out, moving with a great army as her retinue.
565.event: Gandharvadattai sets out from the Silver Mountain with a great armed retinue.

566.reading: Her escort counts a thousand elephants rejoicing at the eye's edge and twice that number of chariots that move through the sky.

567.reading: Horses in golden trappings, able to turn back an army of bowmen, go with her in a number multiplied over the troops already named.
567.nuance: The count in நற்புடைய நாற்றியே is not clear: it may be fourfold the chariots or simply a great many.

568.reading: Young warriors bearing sun-bright spears that the vultures follow, twelve thousand of them, beyond telling, march in the train.

569.reading: When the clouds thunder in the high sky, the elephants trumpet back at them, and the clouds, shaken, cannot pass on.
569.nuance: Who is shaken and cannot go on (அதிர்ந்தவர்க்கு ஏகலாவது இல்லையே) is not fixed by the words; it may be the clouds or anyone who hears.

570.reading: At the roaring of the furious elephants the clouds split their bellies and shed their water in fear.
570.nuance: The army's passage through the sky is made into a storm: the rain is the clouds' terror at the elephants, not weather.

571.reading: The elephants' ichor, mingled with the falling rain, pours down into the deep sea, inside and out.

572.reading: The poet turns to tell what befell the rich man who had grieved when his ship capsized in the wide sea.
572.nuance: The narrator's 'let us tell' (செப்புவாம்) closes the description of the flight and returns to Sridattan, last seen at Kaluzhavegan's court.

573.reading: The milk-white snowy mountain shines whiter still, with gems of blue shadow set in rows all through it.
573.nuance: The verse does not say what it describes; it may be the Silver Mountain the party leaves, or the shining place where the ship is now shown.

574.reading: The great vidyadhara, to the delight of the guileless man's heart, makes known to him that the whole wreck was a deception.
574.event: Dharan reveals to Sridattan that the shipwreck was a trick he staged.
574.nuance: The man deceived is called வஞ்சமின் மனத்தினான், one with no deceit in his mind, in the same verse that names the deceit (வஞ்சம்); the pun sets the guileless merchant against the vidyadhara's ruse.

575.reading: Dharan tells him that because of the maiden's beauty kings with conch-sounding armies thronged everywhere on the cloud-capped Silver Mountain.
575.event: Suitor kings throng the Silver Mountain for Gandharvadattai.

576.reading: The king, with dripping garland, spear and ஆர் flowers on his chest, takes counsel with the astrologer of generous hand, who speaks with grace.
576.event: Kaluzhavegan consults his astrologer about his daughter's marriage.
576.nuance: Which of the two செப்பினான் makes the speaker, the king or the astrologer, is not settled by the line; the next verse is the astrologer's answer.

577.reading: The astrologer declares that the maiden's life lies on the earth, and that therefore the king's beloved friend is even now out on the sea.
577.nuance: These words are the astrologer's, quoted inside Dharan's report. Who நின் காதலான் is cannot be fixed from this verse alone; 578's 'my close friend' suggests Sridattan, the man who will take her to the earth. The verse survives as two long lines.

578.reading: When the astrologer had spoken, Dharan says, the king bade him go and bring his dear friend, and that is how he came that day.
578.event: Kaluzhavegan sends Dharan to fetch Sridattan.

579.reading: Since there is no joy except for those who have first suffered, Dharan says, he bound Sridattan in suffering out of love.

claims.claim: joy comes only to those who have first suffered

579.nuance: The maxim is offered as a deceiver's apology: the suffering was made on purpose, for the joy it would set off. The work does not comment on it here.

580.reading: Saying that he had gained his friend by causing him pain and wishing him long life, Dharan points out the ship he had sunk in the great sea and the companions in it.
580.event: Dharan shows Sridattan the sunken ship and his companions, safe.

581.reading: Cooled within by Dharan's divine words, like rain that brings honey, the spear-bearer with heavy gem earrings answers with a wish that the suffering the vidyadhara lord gave be brought to its end with his own line.
581.nuance: The wish கோன்தரு துன்பம் மற்றென் குலத்தொடு முடிக may mean that such suffering end here, or that a suffering bringing such gain stay with his line to its end; the words allow both.

582.reading: Seeing his friends, Sridattan embraces them with love welling up until his garland is crushed; they tell what they went through on the sea and, clapping their hands, laugh that it was all a play.
582.event: Sridattan embraces his companions, who laugh that their wreck was a play.
582.nuance: நாடகம் turns the wreck that drowned all aboard (512) into a staged show, and the laughter (நக்கார்) comes after the danger, not in it.

583.reading: Like a mountain waterfall poured on a burning wound, the merchant's grief is quenched, and with his dear ones around him and the garlanded maiden he joyfully enters his guarded house in the old city of drums.
583.event: Sridattan comes home to Rajamapuram with Gandharvadattai.

584.reading: As he nears the great house his wife, her brow shining like the crescent, stands bowing like a golden creeper; he raises her, embraces her and takes away the worry from her eyes.
584.event: Sridattan embraces his wife and ends her anxiety.

585.reading: The maiden comes to the maidens' mansion built on a floor of cool moonstone with gold, silver, crystal and coral, its pillars set with gems, and dwells there without distress.
585.event: Gandharvadattai is lodged in the maidens' mansion.

586.reading: After the household duties are done, Sridattan tells his wife, so that she knows it, of the faultless maiden's coming and of what her father has resolved.
586.event: Sridattan tells his wife of Gandharvadattai's arrival and her father's purpose.
586.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 describe a woman resting till her duties are done; whether she is the wife or the maiden, and so to whom Sridattan speaks, depends on reading பாவை in line 3 against the subject of வைகி.

587.reading: His wife consents, and he says that next day they will carry through the rite for the girl whose breasts make even women covet manhood, so that all who see her marvel.
587.event: Sridattan's wife consents and he resolves to begin the marriage rite next day.
587.nuance: கடிவினை is the rite that leads to her marriage; the verse does not yet name the lute contest.

588.reading: Taking much gold and many gems that skilled men had cut from the mountain's belly, the anklet-wearer goes in, sees the ruler and tells him; the king of the spear army grants what he asks, as rule allows.
588.event: Sridattan brings gifts to Kattiyangaran and gains his consent to what he asks for Gandharvadattai.
588.nuance: The verse does not name the king; at this point of the story Rajamapuram's ruler is the usurper Kattiyangaran, and his consent is bought with gems.

links.note: Sridattan told his crew in the storm that their suffering was the ripening of old deeds; Dharan now says the wreck was his own staged deceit.
links.teaches: The epic lets the merchant read the wreck as karma and then shows a planned human cause behind it, so the karmic explanation stands beside an agent's plan rather than replacing it.

links.note: 513 has the sea swallow the merchant's guarded wealth and the loved ones with him; 580 shows the ship and the companions intact.
links.teaches: The loss that the wreck scene narrates as final is revealed as illusion, so the earlier verse's grief was real while its facts were false.

links.note: In the storm Sridattan urged laughter in trouble; after the rescue his companions laugh that the wreck was a play.
links.teaches: The laughter urged as courage before the outcome returns as relief after it, which shows how differently the same laugh weighs once the danger is known to be staged.

links.note: The astrologer's verdict that the maiden's life lies on the earth is what the king turned into his parting saying that daughters, like a conch's pearls, profit those on the earth.
links.teaches: The king's consoling maxim at the parting rests on the astrologer's prophecy told only now, so his resignation is obedience to a foretold fate as well as a father's wisdom.

links.note: The Naladiyar calls those who prattle of astrology the greatest fools; the epic has a king act on an astrologer's word, which proves true.
links.teaches: Two Jain-tradition texts judge the astrologer oppositely: the quatrain dismisses his lore beside the duty death makes urgent, while the epic makes his reading the hinge of its plot. The tension holds only if the quatrain is read as denying astrology's truth, not just its worth.

gains.a: the epic's trust in the astrologer is set against a strand of its own tradition that scorns that lore
gains.b: the quatrain's scorn is shown to stand in a renouncer's frame that a court narrative does not share

links.note: The Naladiyar says friends who share joys but not sorrows do nothing for each other; Dharan inflicts sorrow on his king's friend to give him joy.
links.teaches: The quatrain's test assumes sorrow comes from outside and asks who will share it, while the epic's friend authors the sorrow himself and stands apart from it, a case the rule of sharing does not cover.

gains.a: Dharan's apology is measured against a standard of friendship that his deceit plainly fails
gains.b: the quatrain's rule meets a friend who causes, rather than shares, the grief, which shows its limit

source_issues: 565-576 and 578-580 are short-line verses printed two lines to a line in the source; the tool split them into four lines.
577 survives as two long lines (stanza_length flag): its four short lines were printed in pairs separated by '!' and ',' and were not split; the text itself seems whole.
588 line 4: a TSCII slip (ோ் for ேர்) repaired in நேர்ந்தான்.
